passage:
Class 11 observation note, Disha Menon, class teacher, 14 August
Mehak has had three colds since June. Today she arrived with a flask of strong coffee, her second before first period, she told me. She used to stay back for sitar practice every Wednesday but has skipped it for five weeks. "I don't enjoy it anymore, and there's no time anyway," she said.
In maths she put her head down twice. When I asked about sleep she laughed. "Four hours. It's fine, ma'am. I've just been lazy this term, so I'm studying till two to catch up."
She seemed to truly believe the tiredness was her own fault.
What I did next: I told her that tiredness is a signal, not laziness, and asked her to meet the school counsellor with me on Friday. She agreed, a little reluctantly. I will also call her mother this evening to share what I have seen and ask how things look at home.

qa.q: How many hours of sleep did Mehak say she was getting?
qa.a: Four hours.

qa.q: Why does Mehak keep studying till two despite being so tired?
qa.a: She believes her tiredness means she has been lazy, so she thinks the answer is to push harder.

qa.q: What did Disha Menon do at this stage, and why does it fit?
qa.a: She told Mehak tiredness is a signal, set up a counsellor meeting and planned to call her mother, catching the pattern before it deepens.

qa.q: What might Mehak's mother experience when the teacher calls?
qa.a: She may be surprised or worried to hear about the colds, the coffee and the dropped sitar, and may start to see the late nights at home differently.

grounding: Shows a student running on coffee and late nights, catching repeated colds, losing joy in a hobby and reading exhaustion as laziness.

passage:
Thursday, 11:40 pm
Third cold this term. Nose like a tap, and I still have the organic chem worksheet and two coaching tests.
Drank two cans of cold coffee after school so I could stay up. Hands a bit shaky, but at least I'm awake.
Mridul called at 6 asking if I'd come for football like old times. Said no. Honestly, I didn't even want to. Football used to be the best part of my week and now it feels like one more chore on a list.
Mom asked why I look like a ghost. I said I'm fine.
The truth is I'm slacking. Everyone else manages. If I'm tired it's because I'm soft, so tonight I'm going till 2 and waking at 5:30 to revise.
Just need to push through till the finals.
— Chinmay

qa.q: What did Mridul invite Chinmay to do?
qa.a: To come for football like old times.

qa.q: How does Chinmay explain the tiredness, and what does that reveal?
qa.a: Chinmay thinks being tired means slacking and being soft, which shows exhaustion being mistaken for laziness.

qa.q: What turning point could Chinmay take instead of going till 2?
qa.a: Chinmay could treat the colds, shaky hands and lost love of football as signs to rest, sleep tonight 😴, and tell Mom the truth instead of 'I'm fine'.

qa.q: What might Mridul be feeling after Chinmay says no to football?
qa.a: Mridul may miss the friend who used to love football and wonder whether something is wrong, not just busy.

grounding: Illustrates a student relying on caffeine and late nights, catching colds, losing interest in a hobby and deciding to push harder instead of resting.

passage:
September: Jasleen was topping class tests, running the art club and tutoring after school. She drank two cups of tea to get through evening revision.
October: The tea became coffee, then two coffees. She caught a cold, then another. When her brother Arnab asked her to sketch with him on Sunday, like they always did, she said, "No time. And I'm bored of drawing."
November: She slept through her alarm and missed a test. "I'm just lazy," she told herself, and stayed up till two to make up for it. Arnab found her asleep at the desk at dawn, pen still in her hand, and quietly went to wake their mother.

qa.q: What did Jasleen and Arnab usually do on Sundays?
qa.a: Sketch together.

qa.q: What does Jasleen calling herself lazy suggest?
qa.a: She feels ashamed and frustrated, reading exhaustion as laziness and pushing harder instead of resting.

qa.q: What turning point does Arnab's choice to wake their mother create?
qa.a: It brings a parent in to notice the exhaustion, so Jasleen can get rest and support, and see a doctor if the colds keep coming.

qa.q: What is Arnab experiencing when he finds her asleep at the desk?
qa.a: Arnab seems worried and caring, sad that she has given up drawing and concerned enough to tell their mother.

grounding: Shows a teen running on coffee and late nights, catching colds and losing interest in drawing, reading tiredness as laziness.

passage:
Pallavi beti, you think you need more coffee to study? Let me tell you about me in Class 12.
I was the topper in our town. I wanted to stay the topper. So I drank tea after tea, strong, and studied till three in the morning. I caught every cold going round. I stopped playing the harmonium, which I loved. My friends called, and I said I was busy.
When I felt tired, I thought, Ramesh, you're getting lazy. So I pushed harder.
One day I fell asleep on my bicycle, beta. Right into a ditch. Only then did my father sit me down and make me rest.
Tired is not lazy, Pallavi. Your old uncle learned it the hard way.

qa.q: What instrument did Ramesh stop playing?
qa.a: The harmonium.

qa.q: What was young Ramesh feeling when the word lazy came to mind?
qa.a: Young Ramesh felt ashamed and afraid of losing the topper's place, so tiredness looked like laziness and the answer was to push harder.

qa.q: In the story, what turning point finally made Ramesh rest?
qa.a: Falling asleep on his bicycle into a ditch, after which his father sat him down and made him rest.

qa.q: How might Ramesh's father have felt after the ditch?
qa.a: His father was probably frightened and worried, realising how exhausted his son had become.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling running on tea and late nights as a teen, catching colds and dropping music, reading tiredness as laziness.

passage:
It was the week of prelims, the building's power kept cutting out, and Pradeep had a cold for the third time that month. He studied by phone torchlight with an energy drink he'd bought from the corner shop.
Mridul came over with notes. "Aren't you coming for football?"
"I don't even like football any more."
"Since when?"
"Since there's no time." Pradeep sneezed. "I'm just being lazy. I need to push through."
Mridul looked at the dark circles, the pile of cans, the tissues. "Pradeep, you're not lazy. You're exhausted."
"Same thing."
"It's not." Mridul picked up his phone. "I'm telling your mum you need sleep, not another can."

qa.q: How many times had Pradeep had a cold that month?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he said he doesn't like football any more?
qa.a: He felt drained and flat, too worn out to enjoy things, and ashamed, calling himself lazy.

qa.q: What turning point does Mridul create?
qa.a: By naming exhaustion instead of laziness and telling Pradeep's mum, he brings in an adult so Pradeep can rest and get checked if the colds continue.

qa.q: What is it like for Mridul to see the cans and tissues?
qa.a: Mridul seems worried and protective, alarmed at how run-down his friend has become.

grounding: Shows a teen running on energy drinks and late nights, catching colds and losing interest in football, reading tiredness as laziness.

passage: At 11:40 p.m., at her corner desk in the Chennai flat, Charu made her third cold coffee of the day and stirred it with a pencil. Her nose was running again, the fourth cold since term began. On the shelf her veena sat under a dust cover she had not lifted in six weeks. "You used to play every evening," her sister Vidya said from the doorway. "No time," Charu said. "I'm just being lazy. I wasted the whole afternoon staring at one page." She opened the chemistry guide, determined to finish two chapters before sleeping, and read the same paragraph four times. Vidya watched her pinch her own arm to stay awake, then went quietly to wake their mother.

qa.q: How long had Charu's veena stayed under its dust cover?
qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.q: Why does Charu call herself lazy?
qa.a: She feels frustrated and ashamed of her tiredness, reading exhaustion as laziness, so she pushes harder.

qa.q: What could help Charu at this stage?
qa.a: Seeing the colds, the lost music and the late coffees as signs she needs rest, and talking to a parent or doctor, rather than pushing harder.

qa.q: How does Vidya seem to see Charu's late nights?
qa.a: Vidya is worried, remembering Charu playing every evening, and goes to wake their mother.

grounding: Shows a student running on coffee and late nights, catching colds and dropping hobbies, reading the tiredness as laziness and pushing on.
